issues.legal_issue: A life estate created for a widow by a settlement instrument that expressly limits her interest does not become full ownership under the general enlargement rule when the instrument falls within the statutory exception for restricted estates.
material_facts: A settlement deed granted a widow a life interest in certain properties and provided that they would revert to the settlor or his heirs upon her death.
After the widow died, the settlor’s son claimed the properties under the deed, while the widow’s brother claimed under her will.

The appellant argued that the settlement was in exchange for properties allegedly alienated without authority, and that the widow’s interest in those properties should mean she obtained full title to the settlement properties.
issues.conclusion: The settlement deed created a restricted estate within the statutory exception, so the widow did not acquire full or alienable ownership of the properties. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a woman’s limited interest may be enlarged into full ownership, but section 14(2) is an exception: where an instrument creates a restricted estate, the enlargement under subsection (1) does not apply. The Court relied on these provisions and cited no earlier cases.

predicates.appeal_over_widow_estate: A party appealed a decision resolving competing claims to property after a widow’s death, including a claim based on her will.
predicates.settlement_instrument_created_restricted: A settlor used a settlement instrument to grant a widow a limited interest in property, with the property to revert to the settlor or the settlor’s heirs after her death.
predicates.widow_did_not_acquire_alienable_title: The widow did not acquire full ownership that she could transfer by will.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns competing claims to property after a widow’s death and a settlement instrument gave her only a restricted interest, the widow did not acquire alienable title.
